passages.happening:
The king of the Ammonites dies, and his son Hanun succeeds him. David says, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me” (verse 2), and he sends envoys to console him.

But the Ammonite princes say to Hanun, “Just because David has sent you comforters, do you really believe he is showing respect for your father? Has not David instead sent his servants to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it?” (verse 3).

So Hanun shaves off half of each envoy's beard, cuts their garments off at the hips, and sends them away (verse 4). David sends messengers to meet them, ‘since they had been thoroughly humiliated’. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, around their capital Rabbah, where modern Amman stands. Nahash was the Ammonite king Saul had defeated at Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11). The text does not say what kindness Nahash showed David. A common suggestion is that an enemy of Saul would be a natural friend to Saul's rival, perhaps in David's fugitive years, but that is a guess.

Sending comforters when a king died was a normal courtesy between allied rulers, part of keeping a treaty alive under a new king. The princes' suspicion was not absurd, since envoys did gather intelligence. What made Hanun's answer so provocative was its form. A full beard was a mark of a grown man's dignity, and shaving half of it made each envoy ridiculous. Cutting their garments at the hips exposed them the way captives were stripped and paraded. To insult a king's envoys was to insult the king who sent them, and everyone understood it as an act of war.

David's word to the men is a small act of care. They need not walk into the capital in that state. Jericho was the first town west of the Jordan on the road from Ammon, and they could wait there until they were themselves again.
passages.later: Chronicles tells the same story (1 Chronicles 19:1-5). Isaiah describes captives of Egypt led away by the king of Assyria stripped in the same way, ‘to Egypt’s shame’ (Isaiah 20:4).
passages.asks: Hanun's advisers read kindness as a trick. Ask when you have misjudged someone's good will, and what it cost. And ask how you might protect the dignity of someone who has just been humiliated.

passages.t: Joab and Abishai on two fronts
passages.happening:
‘When the Ammonites realized that they had become a stench to David’ (verse 6), they hire Aramean soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, a thousand men from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand from Tob. David sends Joab with the whole army.

The Ammonites line up at the city gate, while their hired Arameans wait in the open country. Joab sees battle lines before him and behind him. He takes the best men against the Arameans and gives the rest to his brother Abishai against the Ammonites. “If the Arameans are too strong for me,” said Joab, “then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue. Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight” (verses 11-12).

The Arameans flee before Joab, and when the Ammonites see it, they flee before Abishai into the city. Joab returns to Jerusalem (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
‘A stench to David’ is an idiom for becoming hateful to someone. The Ammonites know they have started a war, and they buy an army.

The Arameans were a network of kingdoms in Syria. Beth-rehob and Zobah lay to the north, Maacah near Mount Hermon, and Tob east of the Jordan. Chronicles adds that the Ammonites paid a thousand talents of silver for the chariots they hired.

Joab's speech is the center of the chapter. Facing enemies in front and behind, he splits the army, promises his brother mutual rescue, calls the men to be strong, and leaves the outcome to God. The word for rescue is often used in the Psalms for God's own deliverance, and here it is used of soldiers who owe each other their lives. Joab plans carefully and fights hard, and he does not pretend the result is his to decide.

The story is shaped by one repeated verb, to see. The Ammonites see, Joab sees, the Ammonites see the Arameans flee, the Arameans see that they are beaten, and at the end the vassal kings see it too. Each party reads the situation and acts on what it sees.
passages.later:
Joab's call to be strong echoes the charge given to Joshua before the conquest: ‘Be strong and courageous’ (Joshua 1:6).

Tob was the land where Jephthah once gathered fighting men around him: ‘Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob’ (Judges 11:3). Now its men fight for hire again.
passages.asks: Joab planned carefully and then said, ‘May the LORD do what is good in His sight’. Ask how you hold careful planning and trust in God together. And ask who stands beside you, ready to come to your rescue, and whom you have promised the same.

passages.happening:
The Arameans regroup. Hadadezer sends for more troops from beyond the Euphrates, and they come to Helam under his commander Shobach. David gathers all Israel, crosses the Jordan and meets them at Helam. ‘But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers’ (verse 18), and Shobach is killed too.

‘When all the kings who were subject to Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This chapter tells at length the Aramean wars that chapter 8 summed up in a few lines. Hadadezer of Zobah heads a coalition that can draw troops from beyond the Euphrates. Helam was east of the Jordan, though its exact place is uncertain.

The numbers here differ from the same account in Chronicles, as numbers in copied ancient texts often do. Samuel has seven hundred charioteers and Chronicles seven thousand. And the BSB prints foot soldiers in verse 18 where the Hebrew has horsemen, following the parallel passage. The site's page on the numbers in Samuel and Chronicles sets these out.

The Ammonites are left alone, behind their walls. The war against them is not over. It is still going on at the start of the next chapter, when David stays in Jerusalem while Joab besieges Rabbah. A reader should keep this chapter in mind: the king who sends his army into the field here will soon send one of his own soldiers to his death.
passages.later: Chronicles gives the same battle with a different number: ‘David killed seven thousand of their charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers’ (1 Chronicles 19:18).
passages.asks: The Arameans made peace only when they saw they were beaten. Ask whether there is a quarrel you are keeping up only until you are sure you cannot win it. And ask what it would take to make peace sooner.
